items.stem: Give the name of the enzyme present in the fluid in our mouth cavity. State the gland which produces it. What would happen to the digestion process if this gland stops secreting this enzyme?
items.answer: The enzyme present in the fluid of the mouth cavity is salivary amylase. It is produced by the salivary gland. This enzyme helps in the digestion of starch in the mouth, so if the gland stops secreting it the digestion of starch will stop and this will affect the body negatively. Salivary amylase is a glucose-polymer cleavage enzyme produced by the salivary glands; it forms a small portion of the total amylase, most of which is made by the pancreas.
items.ocr: Printed answer was OCR-garbled ('it will kept are body negatively'); repaired to 'this will affect the body negatively'. Sentence casing restored.

items.stem: What are the functions of food?
items.answer: The functions of food are the following: (i) It provides energy. (ii) It helps in repairing damaged tissues. (iii) It helps in the growth and development of the body.

items.stem: What is diffusion?
items.answer: The movement of molecules from a region of their higher concentration to a region of lower concentration is called diffusion.
items.ocr: Printed 's called diffusion' restored to 'is called diffusion'.

items.stem: What do you mean by 'nutrient'? Or Define the term 'nutrient'.
items.answer: A nutrient is a substance which a living organism, i.e. a plant or an animal, obtains from its surroundings and utilises for the growth of its body, repair of worn out tissues and for getting energy.

items.stem: Define the term nutrition.
items.answer: Nutrition is the procurement of substances for the growth of the body, repair of the worn out tissues and to obtain energy to do work.

items.stem: What is photosynthesis? Mention its importance.
items.answer: Photosynthesis is an important activity of all green plants by which they prepare their own food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of chlorophyll and light energy. Importance: (i) It is the only way of converting solar energy into food (biochemical) energy. (ii) It is the only biological process that releases oxygen into the atmosphere, which supports all life forms on the earth.

items.stem: Which are the first simple molecules of food produced during photosynthesis? What happens to these simple molecules in the leaves later?
items.answer: (i) Glucose molecules are the first simple molecules of food produced during photosynthesis. (ii) These molecules combine to produce starch, which is stored in various parts of the plant.

items.stem: What are the events taking place during photosynthesis?
items.answer: The following events occur during photosynthesis: (i) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll. (ii) Conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. (iii) Reduction of carbon dioxide into carbohydrates.

items.stem: What is the compensation point with relation to the release of CO₂ by the plants?
items.answer: When the intensity of light is low (mainly during morning and evening), the amount of CO₂ released during respiration by plants equals its consumption by photosynthesis. This state is called the compensation point.
items.ocr: LaTeX artefact 'CO $2$' rewritten as CO₂ in both the stem and the answer.

items.stem: What is parasitism? Give two examples of parasites, one from animals and one from plants.
items.answer: Parasitism is an association between two organisms in which one (the parasite) lives in or on and at the expense of the other (the host) and obtains food and shelter from it. The host does not get any benefit from such an association. Cuscuta (amar bel) is a parasitic plant and roundworm (Ascaris) is a parasitic animal.

items.stem: What is the mode of nutrition in fungi? Explain how fungi obtain their food.
items.answer: Fungi obtain their nourishment from dead and decaying organic matter. Such a mode of nutrition is known as saprophytic nutrition. Fungi first give out enzymes over their food which digest it. This digested food is then absorbed by the fungi.
items.ocr: Printed stem is only 'What is the mode of nutrition in fungi?'; the clause 'Explain how fungi obtain their food' was added to keep this two-mark item distinct from the identically worded one-mark question 160 on page 17.

items.stem: Name the different parts of the human alimentary canal in their proper sequence.
items.answer: Buccal cavity → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → jejunum → ileum → caecum → colon → rectum.
items.ocr: MinerU rendered the arrows as '$$' and dropped several of them altogether; all arrows in the sequence were restored as →.

items.stem: Briefly describe the digestive activity in the small intestine of man.
items.answer: The partially digested carbohydrates, proteins and emulsified fat enter the small intestine. The digestive glands in the intestinal wall secrete a juice called succus entericus. Succus entericus contains many enzymes which complete the digestive process as follows: all proteins and peptones are digested into amino acids, all carbohydrates are ultimately digested into glucose, and fat droplets are digested into fatty acids and glycerol.
items.ocr: Stray OCR character 'b' after 'as follows' removed; 'peptone' pluralised to 'peptones' and 'aminoacids' split into 'amino acids'.

items.stem: Write one function each of the salivary glands, liver and pancreas.
items.answer: Salivary glands: they secrete saliva containing ptyalin which digests starch into maltose. Liver: it secretes bile juice which breaks down fats into fat globules. Pancreas: it secretes pancreatic juice which contains protein-digesting and starch-digesting enzymes.
items.ocr: LaTeX artefact '$\therefore$' after 'Salivary glands' was a mis-read colon and was restored as ':'.

items.stem: Explain the process of nutrition in Amoeba with a suitable diagram.
items.answer: Amoeba takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions of the cell surface which surround the food particle and fuse over it, forming a food vacuole. Inside the food vacuole, complex substances are broken down into simpler ones which then diffuse into the cytoplasm. The remaining undigested material is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out of the body.
items.ocr: The diagram is to be drawn by the student in the answer; no printed question figure accompanies this item, so no image is attached.

items.stem: Mention the site of complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in humans.
items.answer: Small intestine in the alimentary canal.

items.stem: Name the process of loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of the plants.
items.answer: Transpiration.

items.stem: Name the component of blood which transports: (i) food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes, (ii) oxygen.
items.answer: (i) Plasma. (ii) Haemoglobin present in RBCs.

items.stem: Name the form in which carbohydrates are stored in plants.
items.answer: Starch.

items.stem: What is emulsification of fat?
items.answer: The breakdown of large fat globules into smaller globules, which are then digested into fatty acids and glycerol.
items.ocr: Printed answer reads 'The breakdown of fat globules into fatty acids and glycerol'; wording expanded slightly for sense while keeping the printed meaning.

items.stem: Identify the category in which the organisms use carbon dioxide and water for making food.
items.answer: Autotrophs.

items.stem: Name the component of blood that helps in the formation of a blood clot in the event of a cut.
items.answer: Platelets.

items.stem: Name the organisms which utilise complex substances that must be broken down into simpler forms.
items.answer: Heterotrophic organisms or heterotrophs, e.g. animals and fungi.

items.stem: Name the cell organelle in which breakdown of pyruvate to give carbon dioxide, water and energy takes place.
items.answer: Mitochondria.

items.stem: When we breathe out, why does the air passage not collapse?
items.answer: The air passage is covered with rings of cartilage which prevent it from collapsing when there is no air in it.
items.ocr: Printed 'breath out' corrected to 'breathe out'.

items.stem: Name the vein which brings blood to the left atrium from the lungs.
items.answer: Pulmonary vein.

items.stem: Name the respiratory pigment in human beings. Where is this pigment present?
items.answer: Haemoglobin, which is present in the red blood corpuscles.

items.stem: Which is the first enzyme to mix with food in the digestive system?
items.answer: Salivary amylase.

items.stem: Name the organelle in which photosynthesis occurs.
items.answer: Photosynthesis occurs in the green coloured plastids called chloroplasts.
items.ocr: Printed 'plastics' corrected to 'plastids'.

items.stem: Which organ synthesises urea?
items.answer: Liver.
items.ocr: The printed answer was OCR-garbled as 'Ans : Synthesis urea.'; the intended answer (the liver synthesises urea) was restored.

items.stem: What prevents the entry of food into the trachea while swallowing?
items.answer: Epiglottis. It covers the opening of the wind pipe during swallowing.

items.stem: Why is the rate of breathing faster in aquatic animals as compared to terrestrial animals?
items.answer: Because the amount of dissolved O₂ in water is less as compared to that in the air of the atmosphere.
items.ocr: LaTeX artefact '$\mathrm{O}_{2}$' rewritten as O₂.

items.stem: What is the mode of nutrition in fungi?
items.answer: Saprophytic or parasitic.

items.stem: What is the location of the kidneys in the body?
items.answer: The kidneys are located on either side of the backbone towards the back of the lower part of the abdominal cavity.

items.stem: Which system is responsible for maintaining osmoregulation and excretion?
items.answer: The urinary system or excretory system.
items.ocr: This one-mark question sits inside the TWO MARKS character range because MinerU interleaved the page-18 column between the page-16 and page-19 two-mark blocks.

items.stem: Give reason why all organisms must excrete.
items.answer: All organisms must excrete because the metabolic wastes are very toxic and will be harmful to the body if stored.

items.stem: Name the excretory organ in human beings.
items.answer: Kidney.

items.stem: Name the excretory unit in human beings.
items.answer: Nephron.

items.stem: What is the shape of the kidney in human beings?
items.answer: In human beings, kidneys are bean-shaped.

items.stem: Where are the kidneys located in the human body?
items.answer: The kidneys are located in the abdomen.

items.stem: What are ureters?
items.answer: Ureters are excretory tubes which come out from each kidney (one tube from one kidney) and open into the urinary bladder.

items.stem: What is the urinary bladder?
items.answer: The urinary bladder is a pear-shaped reservoir that stores urine before it is discharged outside the body.

items.stem: What is the urethra?
items.answer: The urethra is a muscular tube present at the neck of the urinary bladder which throws out urine through an opening at its end, the urinary opening.

items.stem: Name the chief nitrogenous waste product in human urine.
items.answer: Urea.

items.stem: Blood passes through narrow capillaries and develops very high pressure, as a result of which much of the fluid part of the blood is forced out. Where precisely in our kidneys is this process occurring?
items.answer: In the glomerulus of the nephrons.

items.stem: Which is more harmful, urea or ammonia?
items.answer: Ammonia is more harmful.

items.stem: Which of the following contains less nitrogenous waste: the renal vein or the renal artery?
items.answer: The renal vein contains less nitrogenous waste.
items.ocr: No exam-source code was printed for this question.

items.stem: Name the blood vessels which bring waste products to the kidneys.
items.answer: Renal arteries bring waste products to the kidneys.

items.stem: What is the function of the glomerulus?
items.answer: The glomerulus filters the nitrogenous waste and other substances from the blood.

items.stem: A major amount of water is selectively reabsorbed by the tubular part of the nephron. On what factors does the amount of water reabsorbed depend?
items.answer: The amount of water reabsorbed by the nephron depends on (i) the quantity of excess water present in the body, and (ii) the quantity of dissolved waste to be excreted from the body.

items.stem: (a) What are the main toxic wastes that the kidney filters from the blood? (b) Name any two substances which are selectively reabsorbed from the tubules of a nephron.
items.answer: (a) Urea and uric acid. (b) Water, glucose and amino acids.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Excretion is the biological process by which harmful wastes are removed from an organism's body. Reason (R): The mode of excretion is completely same in both unicellular and multicellular organisms. Read the Assertion and Reason carefully and choose the correct option.
items.assertion: Excretion is the biological process by which harmful wastes are removed from an organism's body.
items.reason: The mode of excretion is completely same in both unicellular and multicellular organisms.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion is false but Reason is true.

items.answer: (c) Assertion is true but Reason is false. Excretion is the biological process by which harmful metabolic wastes are removed from the body. The mode of excretion is completely different in unicellular organisms: in unicellular organisms waste products are diffused into the surrounding water through the body surface, while in multicellular organisms specialised organs perform the function of excretion.

items.answer: (a) Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion. The main organ of the human excretory system is the kidney. The major function performed by the kidneys is to remove excess water and nitrogenous wastes from the blood in the form of urine.
items.ocr: The printed Reason read 'Kidneys perform the function of adding water and nitrogenous wastes from the body', which contradicts the key (option a) and the worked solution ('remove excess water and nitrogenous wastes'). The solution wins: 'adding' was treated as an OCR error and restored to 'removing excess'.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Artificial kidney is a device used to remove nitrogenous waste products from the blood through dialysis. Reason (R): Reabsorption does not occur in artificial kidney. Read the Assertion and Reason carefully and choose the correct option.
items.assertion: Artificial kidney is a device used to remove nitrogenous waste products from the blood through dialysis.
items.reason: Reabsorption does not occur in artificial kidney.

options.label: A

options.label: B

items.answer: (c) Assertion is true but Reason is false. Kidney failure can be managed by an artificial kidney. It is a device used to remove nitrogenous waste products from the blood through dialysis. An artificial kidney is different from a natural kidney as the process of reabsorption does not occur in the artificial kidney.
items.ocr: The printed key marks the Reason false, yet the worked solution states that reabsorption does not occur in an artificial kidney (i.e. the Reason statement is factually true). The printed key and option letter (c) were kept as printed and the conflict is recorded here.
